sm: The speaker responds to critics who list Bible verses on slavery, such as Ephesians six, First Timothy six, and First Peter two, among the worst passages in scripture. He cites an atheist writer and a newspaper list that claim the Bible supports slavery. He argues that first-century slavery was often different from the race-based slavery of the Americas, since people became slaves through war, debt, or unpaid taxes. He compares it to modern taxation, prison labor, and the military draft, saying slavery was defined broadly then. He notes that Paul condemned slave traders in First Timothy one, and says instructions for slaves to honor masters fit the wider teaching that Christians submit to governing authorities.

The speaker continues, saying submission to Rome was not an endorsement of the empire, and that Christians are to submit to parents, elders, one another, and authorities unless this conflicts with a command of God. He says God did not create slavery, which was common across ancient civilizations, including Babylon under Hammurabi. He gives an estimate of five to eight million slaves in the Roman Empire, up to a quarter of Italy's population. Paul's stated purpose was that God's name not be blasphemed, and he urged slaves to seek freedom if they could. The speaker argues that as masters became Christians they would treat slaves justly, so the gospel would eventually end cruel captivity. He closes by saying atheism lacks grounds to call slavery objectively evil.
